nameStory: The name 'cod' comes from the Old English word 'codde,' meaning bag or pouch, likely referring to the fish's rounded, bag-like body shape. Atlantic cod has been such an important fish that it's simply called 'cod' in most places, earning the scientific name 'morhua' from an old Norse word meaning 'cod fish.'
description: Atlantic cod is a chunky, torpedo-shaped fish with a distinctive beard-like barbel hanging from its chin. These brown or greenish fish are covered in darker spots and can grow quite large - typically reaching 3-4 feet long, though some giants have been caught over 6 feet! They're one of New England's most famous fish, historically supporting entire fishing communities for centuries.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Look for the single fleshy barbel (whisker) dangling from the chin - it feels soft and flexible when touched, like a small worm

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Stocky, torpedo-shaped body that feels solid and muscular, with a slightly compressed but robust build

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Three separate dorsal fins on the back and two anal fins underneath - count them to distinguish from other fish

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brown to olive-green back with darker spots, fading to silvery-white belly, with a prominent pale stripe running along each side

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Usually 2-4 feet long when caught, with a hefty weight that feels substantial in your hands

habitat: Atlantic cod live in the cold waters off New England's coast, from shallow nearshore areas down to depths of 1,000 feet along the continental shelf. They prefer rocky bottoms and structured areas where they can hunt for crabs, worms, and smaller fish. You'll find them anywhere from just offshore to far out on traditional fishing grounds like Georges Bank.

seasonality.spring: Cod move into shallower waters for spawning, making them more accessible to shore-based anglers. This is peak fishing season in many areas.
seasonality.summer: Adults often move to deeper, cooler waters but can still be found in productive fishing areas. Younger cod may remain in shallower waters.
seasonality.fall: Cod begin moving back toward shore and feeding heavily to prepare for winter. Colors may appear more vibrant during active feeding periods.
seasonality.winter: Many cod remain in deeper offshore waters, though some can be caught in deeper coastal areas during this quieter fishing season.

funFact: Atlantic cod were so abundant that early explorers claimed you could walk across their backs in some areas, and they literally built New England - the profits from cod fishing funded many coastal towns and even helped finance the American Revolution!
confusionNotes: Atlantic cod are most often confused with haddock, but cod have that distinctive chin barbel while haddock don't, and haddock have a dark 'thumbprint' spot behind their gills that cod lack. Remember: 'Cod have chin whiskers, haddock have thumbprints.'
contextualKnowledge: Atlantic cod are listed as vulnerable due to overfishing - the famous cod collapse of the 1990s saw populations drop by over 95%. Many areas still have strict fishing regulations, so always check current rules before fishing. The cod you might catch today are part of slowly recovering populations.
compareHints: As the only Gadus species commonly found in New England waters, Atlantic cod can be distinguished from other cod family members by their chin barbel (which pollock and haddock lack) and their three dorsal fins. They're generally larger and more robust than their cousins, with that characteristic spotted pattern that gives them excellent camouflage on rocky bottoms.
